identity.method_name: Sentinel-1 Ground Range Detected (GRD) C-band SAR backscatter thresholding for open-water mapping, using the Google Earth Engine dataset COPERNICUS/S1_GRD
identity.family: data-source (paired with a geospatial-rule thresholding step, e.g. Otsu or a fixed dB cut, to turn backscatter into a water/not-water mask -- structurally the same paradigm as the project's current MNDWI>0 rule, just on radar backscatter instead of an optical index)
identity.core_idea: Sentinel-1 is a C-band (5.405 GHz) synthetic aperture radar that images day/night and through cloud cover, unlike Sentinel-2's optical sensor. Calm open water acts as a smooth, specular reflector that scatters almost all incident radar energy away from the sensor, so it appears as a very low-backscatter (dark) region in VV-polarised imagery, in contrast to rough vegetated or built-up land which backscatters strongly; a threshold (fixed dB cut or Otsu bimodal-histogram split) on the VV band separates the two classes. Because SAR is unaffected by cloud, the same lake can in principle be imaged many times per year instead of the project's current one dry-season optical scene per year, turning the annual water-area series from 7 points per lake into potentially dozens.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Threshold rule -- fully unsupervised, exactly the same strategy category as the project's existing MNDWI>0 (Xu 2006) rule, just applied to SAR backscatter (dB) instead of an optical spectral index. No encroachment label of any kind is needed to compute a water mask; the cost is entirely in choosing and defending a threshold value (or an Otsu-style automatic split) rather than in acquiring labels. This does not touch the project's separate, unsolved problem of having no encroachment ground truth at all (limitation 3) -- it only supplies a denser water-area series, the same open question the current classical method already has about whether 'water area' by itself is evidence of encroachment.
fit_to_project.input_required: Per-scene VV (and optionally VH) backscatter in dB over each lake's footprint, plus the incidence-angle band GEE provides alongside it. This is new data the project does not currently have -- it must be acquired from the COPERNICUS/S1_GRD collection via the Earth Engine API for MGRS-43PGQ / the six lake footprints, for the full 2019-2025 window (or back to 2014-10-03, the collection's start date, if the study window is later extended).
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: only-if-reframed, and unlike most other items in this project the reframing is a genuine positive here, not a mitigation. Sentinel-1 revisits the equator roughly every 12 days per single satellite (6 days with both S1A and S1B operating together), which for the 2019-2025 window would yield on the order of 25-30 scenes/year/lake with both satellites and roughly half that with one [uncertain -- the exact per-tile acquisition count for MGRS-43PGQ was not queried against the live Copernicus Data Space catalogue in this research pass; treat the 25-30/year figure as an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a confirmed count, and mark verify before using it in a report]. Reframed to one row per lake per acquisition date, the effective sample size for a lake-level time series rises from 7 to plausibly 100-200 observations over the study window -- and because that same denser series is exactly what the project's own break-detection item (BFAST/Pettitt, id C9) needs to become statistically valid, this item and that one are directly linked: SAR is arguably the only realistic way to lift the project out of the n=7 problem for that test. It does NOT, however, increase the 42-row lake-YEAR tabular dataset itself unless the schema is explicitly redefined to a finer time step; if the annual table is kept as the unit of analysis, this item only supplies a better-estimated (denser, cloud-independent) input to each of those same 42 annual rows, not more rows.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes. Thresholding backscatter into water/not-water requires no labels, in the same way the current MNDWI rule requires none.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Yes, favourably. COPERNICUS/S1_GRD in Earth Engine is offered at 10, 25 or 40 m pixel spacing (Interferometric Wide swath GRD products are commonly used at 10 m); this is finer than or equal to the project's 20 m EPSG:32643 working grid, so downsampling to 20 m is straightforward and loses no information the project would otherwise have used, unlike a case where a sub-metre-trained model is forced onto 20 m Sentinel-2 data. The one genuinely coarse companion band is the per-scene incidence-angle layer, delivered at 20,000 m (i.e. one value per scene, not a real per-pixel measurement) -- this cannot be used as a per-pixel correction and any incidence-angle normalisation has to come from an external DEM-based approach instead.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Primarily fixes limitation (4): one optical scene per year shows only the dry-season minimum, whereas cloud-penetrating SAR can image the same lake repeatedly through the wet season and reveal the actual within-year water-level trajectory (fill, drawdown, refill), not just a single dry-season snapshot. As a direct downstream consequence it also materially helps limitation (1) -- the 42-row/7-year-point sample-size problem -- specifically for time-series statistics, because a lake with 25-30 SAR observations/year gives the BFAST/Mann-Kendall/Pettitt tests in item C9 a real chance of being validly powered instead of disqualified by n=7. It does not touch limitation (2) (static OSM buildings) and does not by itself resolve limitation (3) (no ground truth), since a denser water-area series is still not an encroachment label.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: Partially, and this is the item's strongest genuine argument. With only one point per year, a drained-then-refilled lake (Bellandur: 15.7 ha 2019 -> 0.4 ha 2021 -> 107.9 ha 2025) is indistinguishable from a real multi-year decline if the single annual capture happens to land during the low or high part of the cycle. With 25-30 points per year, a genuine desilting drain-and-refill event should show up as a sharp V-shaped dip WITHIN a single year followed by recovery, which is a qualitatively different, and far more diagnostic, shape than a slow monotonic decline spread across several years -- something a single annual snapshot can never distinguish. The important caveat: SAR does not solve this for free. A freshly drained, wet, silt-flat lakebed is itself a smooth surface and can produce LOW backscatter that a naive VV threshold will misclassify as 'water' when it is actually exposed, saturated mud -- i.e. the exact desilting scenario this item is meant to help with is also a plausible source of new false positives, and this must be explicitly tested (e.g. against known desilting-tender dates) rather than assumed away.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: Potentially yes, and this is the item's most novel proposed advantage over the optical baseline, but it is not yet demonstrated for this project's lakes and should be labelled a hypothesis, not a confirmed result. Dense floating vegetation mats such as water hyacinth present a rough, complex canopy above the water surface, which is expected to raise backscatter (via volume scattering and double-bounce off stems/leaves) relative to the very low, near-noise-floor backscatter of smooth open water beneath it -- the same physical mechanism that lets longer-wavelength SAR distinguish flooded forest from open water in wetland literature. If this holds for hyacinth on Bengaluru's lakes it would be a genuine improvement over optical NDVI, which currently classifies all of Bellandur's and Varthur's hyacinth mats as generic 'vegetation' and hides them from the water-area total (Bellandur 2019: 16 ha water vs 260 ha vegetation in a 315 ha footprint). No Sentinel-1-specific hyacinth backscatter threshold or validated study for these lakes was confirmed during this research pass [uncertain -- a general SAR/floating-macrophyte physical mechanism is well established in wetland remote sensing, but a Bengaluru- or hyacinth-specific SAR threshold or accuracy figure was not located and confirmed against a primary source]. The published Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte-cover mapping (MDPI Remote Sensing 2020, doi 10.3390/rs12223843) is the natural independent cross-check to validate any SAR-derived hyacinth/open-water split against, since that paper's own mapping used optical/NDVI-based methods and would provide an independent reference extent, not a circular one.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None gained. A SAR-derived water mask, however dense in time, still has to be intersected with SOME boundary polygon to produce a buffer-scale statement, and by default that would remain the OpenStreetMap proxy polygon (project_constraints.lake_boundary), which is not a legal reference. The genuine benefit here is temporal, not spatial: having dozens of dates per year lets a buffer-encroachment test (whichever legal buffer distance is used -- the 30 m distance the project note specifies, traceable at various points to the Karnataka Tank Conservation and Development Authority Act s.12(3) and the Bengaluru Master Plan, versus the now-set-aside 75 m NGT figure) be evaluated at many dates instead of one, which is a real statistical-power improvement, but it does not itself supply a more authoritative boundary or buffer source than whatever is already chosen elsewhere in the project.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: This is exactly the field this item is meant to fix, and unlike the OpenStreetMap building count, the underlying physical quantity (VV/VH backscatter) genuinely does change from acquisition to acquisition and is not held constant by data-provider convention. The caveat is that the ACHIEVED density depends on Sentinel-1's real acquisition history over this specific tile, which changed materially across the project's 2019-2025 window: Sentinel-1B failed on 23 December 2021 (power-supply anomaly) and its mission end was formally declared on 3 August 2022, after which only Sentinel-1A provided coverage (roughly a 12-day repeat cycle instead of 6) until Sentinel-1C launched on 5 December 2024 and the two-satellite constellation was re-established around May 2025 (with a 1-day-shifted repeat pattern relative to the original A/B pair). Concretely: 2019-2021 (up to Dec) likely had denser, 6-day-class coverage; from 2022 through early 2025 the project's own study years had roughly half that density; 2025 partially recovers to two-satellite coverage. This step-change in revisit density falling squarely inside the project's own 2019-2025 window must be disclosed explicitly rather than assumed constant.

implementation.libraries: Google Earth Engine Python API (`earthengine-api`) with `geemap` for reading COPERNICUS/S1_GRD and exporting per-lake statistics; no local heavy compute needed since calibration and terrain correction are already applied server-side. `scikit-image` (`skimage.filters.threshold_otsu`) or `numpy` for the thresholding step itself; `rasterio`/`geopandas` for zonal extraction against the lake polygons. If a full offline SAR preprocessing pipeline is instead built from raw products (not necessary given the GEE ARD route below), SNAP/`snappy` or the `s1_ard` GEE processing chain of Mullissa et al. 2021 would be the relevant tools.
implementation.pretrained_weights: Not applicable for a threshold-based (Otsu/fixed-dB) water mask -- no model is trained or fine-tuned. If a CNN-based SAR water segmentation model were substituted instead (a different item), that would require separately sourced weights trained on SAR imagery, which is a materially different (and larger) undertaking than the thresholding approach evaluated here.
implementation.licence: Sentinel-1 data is released under the Copernicus open and free data policy; Earth Engine catalogue access is free for research/non-commercial use under Google's Earth Engine terms. scikit-image (BSD-3), numpy (BSD), rasterio (BSD), geopandas (BSD) are all academic-safe.
implementation.compute_requirement: Low. All radiometric calibration, thermal-noise removal and terrain correction (against SRTM 30 or ASTER DEM for latitudes beyond +/-60 deg) are already applied server-side by Earth Engine's ingestion pipeline before the data is ever pulled to the student's machine, so this runs comfortably on a laptop CPU via the Earth Engine Python API, well inside free Earth Engine quotas; no GPU or Colab/Kaggle credit is required for the thresholding step itself.
implementation.student_days: Roughly 3-5 student-days to pull the COPERNICUS/S1_GRD VV(+VH) series for all six lakes across 2019-2025, apply an Otsu or fixed-dB threshold, sanity-check the result against the existing optical MNDWI mask on temporally close cloud-free dates, and produce the resulting denser water-area series. This is a large discount versus building a full offline SAR preprocessing chain from raw Level-1 products with manual radiometric terrain flattening and speckle filtering (a multi-week, 8-12 student-day undertaking per the workflow documented in Mullissa et al. 2021, Remote Sensing 13(10):1954, doi 10.3390/rs13101954 [verify exact effort figures against that paper directly; the qualitative claim that GEE's ARD product substantially reduces preprocessing burden versus an offline SNAP-based pipeline is well established, but a specific day-count was not confirmed against the primary source in this pass]). An additional 1-2 days should be budgeted for border-noise cleanup and a light speckle-reduction step (a temporal median/mean composite across the many available acquisitions is a low-cost, effective option given the revisit density this item unlocks, and is cheaper than a spatial Lee/Refined-Lee filter).

evaluation.metrics: No accuracy metric can be computed against ground truth because none exists for encroachment, and none exists either for a 'true' per-date water extent. The available, defensible metrics are: (a) internal cross-consistency between the SAR-derived mask and the existing optical MNDWI mask on dates that are cloud-free and close in time (IoU or area-difference, reported as agreement, not accuracy); (b) the number of usable observations per lake-year before and after adding SAR, which is the honest headline metric for this item since its real contribution is density, not per-date precision; (c) the resulting statistical power gained for the break-detection tests in item C9 (e.g. whether Mann-Kendall/Pettitt now clear commonly cited minimum-n thresholds of roughly 8-10 observations, which they could not at the current n=7).
evaluation.validation_protocol: Leave-one-lake-out for any threshold or model choice tuned across the six lakes, to avoid overfitting a single dB cut-point to the specific mix of lake surfaces seen in the study. Because SAR acquisitions of the same lake only 6-12 days apart are highly autocorrelated, a naive random split across dates within a lake would leak essentially identical conditions between train and 'test' dates -- any date-level validation should be leave-one-year-out or a block hold-out with a buffer of at least one repeat cycle between train and test dates, not a simple random shuffle of individual scenes.
evaluation.leakage_risk: The dominant risk is temporal autocorrelation: adjacent 6-12 day SAR acquisitions of the same lake are not independent samples, so any split that treats them as such will understate real generalisation error. A second, project-specific risk is threshold leakage: if the VV/VH dB cut-point is chosen by eye after looking at all six lakes' full multi-year series (including, e.g., knowing in advance that Bellandur was drained in 2021), the threshold will be implicitly tuned to reproduce the already-known Bellandur story rather than independently discovering it -- any such tuning should be disclosed, or the threshold should be fixed using an automatic method (Otsu) applied per-scene rather than hand-picked.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: The added observation density is exactly what makes proper uncertainty reporting possible for the first time: with 25-30+ points per lake-year, a within-year mean water area can be reported with a genuine standard deviation or bootstrap confidence interval, instead of the single point estimate the current one-scene-per-year method is limited to. This should be treated as a mandatory addition, not an optional nicety, since it is one of this item's few unambiguous, low-risk wins.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not applicable in the sense of synthetic data generation, but a closely related honesty risk exists: any interpolation used to fill gaps between real SAR acquisitions (e.g. during the reduced single-satellite 2022-2024 window) must be clearly and separately labelled as interpolation and never presented as an additional real observation, exactly as flagged for the break-detection item (C9).

evidence.published_performance: SAR-based water/flood mapping using VV-threshold or Otsu-style approaches on Sentinel-1 GRD is a well-established, widely used technique in the flood-mapping literature (e.g. the automated processing chains of Twele et al. 2016, International Journal of Remote Sensing, and Chini et al. 2017, IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing, 'A Hierarchical Split-Based Approach for Parametric Thresholding of SAR Images: Flood Inundation as a Test Case' [verify exact DOIs and reported accuracy figures against the primary papers directly; specific overall-accuracy or IoU numbers were not independently re-confirmed in this research pass and should not be quoted without checking the source]. Google Earth Engine's own COPERNICUS/S1_GRD preprocessing (thermal noise removal, radiometric calibration, terrain correction using SRTM 30/ASTER) is documented on the dataset's official catalogue page (https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/COPERNICUS_S1_GRD), and known residual deficiencies in that default pipeline (incomplete border-noise removal, geometric-only terrain correction with no radiometric terrain flattening) are documented in Mullissa, A. et al. (2021), 'Sentinel-1 SAR Backscatter Analysis Ready Data Preparation in Google Earth Engine', Remote Sensing 13(10):1954, doi 10.3390/rs13101954 [verify -- this paper's existence and general subject matter is asserted with reasonable confidence from training knowledge, but its specific findings could not be re-confirmed by fetching the primary source in this research pass because mdpi.com returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches].
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: The cited flood-mapping and ARD-preprocessing methodology papers were developed and validated on flood events and general SAR backscatter analysis at regional/global scale (e.g. European and other flood case studies), not on small urban lakes, and not on Bengaluru specifically.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No peer-reviewed application of Sentinel-1 SAR water detection specifically to Bengaluru lake encroachment monitoring was confirmed during this research pass. Sentinel-1-based flood mapping has been applied elsewhere in India (e.g. Kerala 2018, Assam/Bihar riverine floods, commonly via ISRO/NRSC and academic groups), but this is generic large-scale flood mapping, not small-urban-lake, buffer-scale, or Bengaluru-specific work [uncertain -- an exhaustive literature search for a Bengaluru-lake-specific SAR study was not possible in this research pass since the web-search tool budget was exhausted partway through; only targeted document fetches were available].
evidence.evidence_recency: The Sentinel-1 mission has been continuously operating since 2014-10-03 (per the COPERNICUS/S1_GRD catalogue start date); the core flood-mapping/thresholding methodology literature cited is 2016-2021; the Sentinel-1B failure (23 Dec 2021), its formal mission end (3 Aug 2022) and the Sentinel-1C launch (5 Dec 2024) are current, recent facts directly confirmed for this research pass via Wikipedia and ESA's Sentinel-1 mission documentation (sentiwiki.copernicus.eu). None of the item's central claims rest solely on pre-2020 evidence.
evidence.primary_sources: COPERNICUS/S1_GRD Earth Engine catalogue page: https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/COPERNICUS_S1_GRD (fetched and confirmed in this research pass: preprocessing steps, resolution options, polarisations, revisit cadence, data start date). ESA Sentinel-1 mission documentation (sentiwiki.copernicus.eu/web/s1-mission) confirming the equatorial 6-day two-satellite / 12-day single-satellite repeat cycle and the post-S1B-failure observation-scenario adjustment (fetched and confirmed). Wikipedia 'Sentinel-1' article confirming the Sentinel-1B failure date (23 Dec 2021), mission-end declaration (3 Aug 2022) and Sentinel-1C launch date (5 Dec 2024) (fetched and confirmed; treated as a secondary but currently reliable source for these specific, verifiable dates). Mullissa et al. 2021, Remote Sensing 13(10):1954, doi 10.3390/rs13101954 (S1 ARD preprocessing gaps -- cited from training knowledge, not independently re-confirmed this pass; mark verify). Twele et al. 2016 and Chini et al. 2017 (SAR flood/water thresholding methodology -- cited from training knowledge, exact DOIs and figures not independently re-confirmed this pass; mark verify). Macrophyte cross-check reference: MDPI Remote Sensing 2020, doi 10.3390/rs12223843 (Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte-cover mapping, already cited in the project's own field definitions; full text could not be fetched in this pass, mdpi.com returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so its specific methodology/findings are reproduced here only from the project's own prior internal citations, not independently re-verified).

risk.failure_modes: (1) A freshly desilted, wet, smooth lakebed can produce low VV backscatter and be misclassified as water, meaning SAR does not automatically resolve, and could in some cases worsen, the exact desilting-vs-encroachment ambiguity it is being proposed to help with. (2) Radar shadow and layover behind tall structures in dense urban settings produce dark regions that a naive threshold can confuse with water; Bengaluru's built environment around several of these lakes (IT-corridor towers near Bellandur/Varthur, dense mid-rise construction elsewhere) makes this a real, non-trivial risk, though likely less severe than in a true high-rise-canyon city, since much of Bengaluru's density is mid-rise rather than skyscraper-dense [uncertain -- no site-specific shadow/layover quantification for these six lakes was performed in this research pass]. (3) Wind-roughened open water during the monsoon season raises backscatter and can cause false NEGATIVES (missed water), the mirror-image error to the shadow/smooth-surface false positive. (4) The Sentinel-1B outage (Dec 2021-2024) means the project's own 2022-2024 study years have materially sparser SAR coverage than 2019-2021 or the recovering 2025, so the promised gain in observation density is not uniform across the study window and must be reported per-year, not as a single blanket figure. (5) Asphalt, bare soil, and other smooth dry surfaces adjacent to the lakes remain a known general SAR-water false-positive source, structurally the same category of error as the desilted-lakebed case above.
risk.panel_defensibility: The defensible position is to state plainly that SAR does not solve the 'no ground truth' problem (limitation 3) at all -- it is still an unsupervised threshold, structurally identical in that respect to the current MNDWI rule -- and that its real, defensible contribution is temporal density: turning an n=7 annual series into a much denser one that (a) can, for the first time, be run through Mann-Kendall/Pettitt with a defensible sample size, and (b) can show whether a given year's water dip has the V-shaped, within-year, drain-and-recover SHAPE of desilting or the flatter, multi-year, monotonic shape of progressive loss. A panel asking 'how do you know your SAR water mask is right' should be met with the honest cross-check against the optical mask on coincident dates (an agreement statistic, not an accuracy statistic) and an explicit list of the known urban/smooth-surface/shadow failure modes above, not a claim of superior accuracy that cannot be substantiated without ground truth.
risk.honest_expectation: This will not produce a demonstrably more accurate single water mask than the existing optical MNDWI rule -- both share the same fundamental problem of being physically-motivated thresholds with no ground truth to calibrate or validate against, and SAR introduces its own new failure modes (shadow, smooth wet mud, wind roughening) in place of optical's own (cloud gaps, hyacinth-as-vegetation). Its realistic, defensible value is structural: converting the project's single dry-season snapshot per year into a genuinely denser, cloud-independent time series that makes previously-disqualified statistical tests (BFAST/Mann-Kendall/Pettitt) usable, and that gives a real, if imperfect, chance at telling a desilting dip apart from a progressive decline by its within-year shape rather than by hoping a single annual capture landed on the informative date.

verdict.recommended_rank: adopt-if-time -- the revisit-frequency gain and its direct link to fixing the project's currently-disqualified time-series break-detection tests (item C9) make this one of the highest-value additions available to the project, but the extra engineering (threshold calibration, cross-checking against optical, disclosing the Sentinel-1B-outage-driven density gap in 2022-2024, and honestly testing rather than assuming away the desilted-lakebed and urban-shadow false-positive risks) is real and should not be understated.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We added Sentinel-1 SAR (COPERNICUS/S1_GRD) because it can image lakes through cloud roughly every 6-12 days instead of once a year, which is what finally gives our break-detection tests enough points to be statistically valid and lets us tell a same-year desilting dip apart from a slow multi-year decline by its shape, while being upfront that dense Bengaluru terrain and freshly-drained lakebeds create their own new false-positive risks that we tested for rather than assumed away.
